nameStory: This bee gets its "bicolored" name from the striking difference between males and females - males sport bright yellow and black stripes while females shimmer with metallic green heads and thoraxes. The "sweat bee" part comes from their habit of landing on sweaty humans to lap up salt and moisture, though they're gentle and rarely sting unless handled roughly.
description: The Bicolored Striped Sweat Bee is a small, eye-catching native pollinator about the size of a honeybee. Males are unmistakable with their bold yellow and black striped abdomens and metallic green heads, while females have entirely metallic green bodies that gleam like tiny emeralds in sunlight. These gentle bees are important pollinators that nest underground in small colonies, with several females often sharing the same burrow entrance. You'll often spot them visiting flowers in gardens, meadows, and woodland edges throughout the warmer months.

idTips.label: Male coloration
idTips.description: Males have brilliant metallic green-blue heads and thoraxes with bright yellow and black banded abdomens that catch the eye from several feet away

idTips.label: Female coloration
idTips.description: Females are entirely metallic green with a jewel-like shimmer that changes from emerald to blue-green as they move in the light

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: About half an inch long with a compact, robust build similar to a small honeybee but with a more tapered abdomen

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Quick, darting flight with frequent hovering near flowers, often making a soft buzzing sound as they work

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Gentle and focused on flowers, may briefly land on skin to collect moisture but flies away quickly without aggression

idTips.label: Ground nesting
idTips.description: Look for small burrow holes in bare or sparsely vegetated soil where multiple bees may be entering and exiting

habitat: Found in diverse open and semi-open habitats including gardens, meadows, woodland edges, and parks throughout New England. They prefer areas with abundant flowers near suitable nesting sites - well-drained, sandy or loamy soil that's easy to excavate. Often seen in suburban areas where they nest in garden beds, lawn edges, or bare patches of earth.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, with peak activity starting in May as early wildflowers and fruit trees bloom.
seasonality.summer: Most active period from June through August when both males and females are commonly seen visiting flowers. Peak nesting activity occurs during this time.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall, especially on warm September days when late-season flowers like asters and goldenrod are blooming.
seasonality.winter: Adults die with the first hard frosts, leaving only mated females or larvae overwintering underground in their burrows.

funFact: This humble bee holds the distinguished title of being the official bee of Toronto, Canada - making it one of the few insects to receive municipal recognition for its ecological importance!
confusionNotes: The metallic green females might be confused with other sweat bees, but the males are unmistakable with their yellow-striped abdomens. Remember: "Green head, yellow rear = bicolored male here!" Other male sweat bees typically lack this dramatic yellow striping.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "sweat bees," these insects are actually beneficial pollinators that only occasionally visit humans for moisture. They're much less aggressive than wasps or hornets and their gentle nature makes them wonderful garden companions rather than pests to avoid.
compareHints: Among its striped sweat bee relatives, the Bicolored Striped Sweat Bee is the most commonly encountered in New England. The Silky Striped Sweat Bee males have more silvery-white stripes rather than bright yellow, while Brown-winged Striped Sweat Bee males show darker wing coloration. The Bicolored's brilliant yellow striping on males makes it the most vivid of the group.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Agapostemon relatives, the Silky Striped Sweat Bee has the most pronounced metallic green coloration on the head and thorax.
